title: Making the delivery promise visible on the product page
summary: DEMO CONTENT — a representative case study used to build and test the template. All numbers are placeholders, not real results.
role: Lead UX/UI & CRO Designer — research, hypothesis, design, test QA, readout

cover.alt: Demo wireframe of a product page with a delivery-date line highlighted below the price

body: This is demo content. It shows how a real project would be structured: a personalised product with a multi-step configurator, sold mostly on mobile, with strong seasonal peaks.
As the designer on the conversion team I owned the problem from discovery to readout, working with a PM, one developer and an analyst.

challenge.question: Why do mobile visitors who reach the product page add to cart, then leave at shipping?
body: Demo narrative: drop-off between cart and checkout rose during peak season. Delivery information lived in a collapsed accordion below the fold, and only appeared as a date at checkout.
The business needed to know whether delivery uncertainty — not price — was the main blocker before investing in faster fulfilment.

findings.title: Visitors look for delivery information and can't find it
findings.detail: Demo finding: in a sample of recordings, mobile users scrolled to the footer and back before abandoning.

findings.title: "When will it arrive?" is the most common pre-purchase question
findings.detail: Demo finding: delivery timing dominates pre-purchase support contacts during peak season.

findings.title: Delivery copy uses internal language
findings.detail: "Production time + shipping time" forces customers to do date maths.

hypothesis.if: we show a concrete estimated delivery date directly below the price on mobile product pages
hypothesis.then: more visitors who add to cart will proceed through checkout
hypothesis.because: recordings and support tickets indicate delivery uncertainty, not price, is the main reason for hesitation in peak season
rationale: Isolated to one change (date placement + format) so the result can be attributed.
Mobile only: that is where the accordion is furthest below the fold.
Guardrail on return rate to make sure we don't over-promise.

body: Three directions were explored before choosing the one that isolates the idea best.

options.name: A — Countdown timer
options.reason: Adds urgency as a second variable; hard to attribute the effect.

options.name: B — Date below price
options.description: A single line: "Estimated delivery: Fri, 12 Dec".
options.reason: Smallest change that answers the user's question at the decision point.

options.name: C — Delivery calculator
options.reason: Higher effort; revisit if B shows a signal.

after.alt: Demo wireframe, after: estimated delivery date shown as one line directly below the price

experiment.duration: Demo · 3 weeks, two full business cycles
experiment.audience: Mobile visitors on product pages, all traffic sources
details: Sample size calculated up front for a minimum detectable effect; runtime fixed in advance, no peeking-based stopping.
Variant QA'd on a device matrix before launch, including long date strings in other locales.
Delivery date computed server-side from the same source as checkout so both always match.

results.summary: Demo outcome: the primary metric moved in the expected direction, but the order-level effect was inconclusive.

metrics.label: Checkout start rate
metrics.note: Placeholder. Replace with the verified value from the research workflow.

results.decision: Demo decision: ship the date line to 100% (no harm on guardrails, clear user benefit) and test the parked postcode calculator next.

failedAssumptions.assumption: Showing the date would lift add-to-cart.
failedAssumptions.reality: Demo: add-to-cart didn't move. The date mattered after the decision to buy, not before it.
Demo: in follow-up interviews, they wanted a reliable date before a specific occasion, not the fastest one.

iterations.label: v1
iterations.outcome: Demo: primary metric up, orders inconclusive.

iterations.label: v2
iterations.change: Occasion framing: "Arrives before Christmas" in peak season

lessons: Put the answer where the question is asked — at the price, not in the footer.
A metric moving mid-funnel doesn't guarantee an order-level effect; plan for both.
Ask why a date matters. "Before the occasion" is a different promise from "fast".
